seo.title: Repotting a Plant: Step-by-Step Guide and Pot Size (2026)
seo.description: Repot a houseplant in 8 steps: spot a root-bound plant, pick a pot 1 to 2 inches wider, loosen the roots and water in. Extension-sourced, pot calculator, 2026.
seo.h1: How to repot a plant: signs, timing, pot size and the steps

answer: Repot in spring or early summer, when the plant is growing. Pick a pot 1 or 2 inches wider with a drainage hole, slide the plant out, loosen or cut circling roots, set it at the same depth in fresh potting mix, press gently and water until it drains.
intro: Repotting is less about giving a plant more room than about giving its roots fresh mix and the right amount of it. Clemson HGIC says fast growers may need a new pot every year while slow growers can wait two or three, and some plants, amaryllis among them, actually do better potbound. Two mistakes cause much of the trouble: timing and size. Moving a plant while it is dormant, sick or starting to flower stresses it when it cannot respond, and jumping to a much larger pot surrounds the roots with wet soil they cannot use. Both Clemson HGIC and the Illinois Extension agree on the method: repot during active growth, go only 1 or 2 inches wider, keep the plant at its original depth, and water thoroughly right after. The calculator below turns that rule into a pot size and the amount of mix to buy.

sections.h2: Five signs a plant is ready for a bigger pot
paras: The Illinois Extension lists the signals worth acting on. Clemson HGIC adds one more test: turn the plant out of its pot, and if the roots form a solid mass around the outside of the root ball, it needs repotting.
list: Roots are growing out through the drainage hole.
Roots show on the soil surface.
The pot is filled with roots and little mix is visible.
New leaves come in smaller than normal.
The plant wilts between its normal waterings, or, as Clemson puts it, needs frequent watering or wilts shortly after being watered.

sections.h2: When to repot, and when to wait
paras: Spring and early summer are the window. The Illinois Extension says repotting goes best while the plant is actively growing, and Clemson HGIC suggests checking the roots when new growth starts in spring. Clemson is just as clear about when not to do it: never repot an ailing plant, a dormant one, or one that is beginning to flower. A plant that looks sick is usually reacting to water, light or pests, and a new pot adds stress without fixing any of those. The one real emergency is root rot, which has its own procedure in our root rot guide.

Cacti follow their own calendar. Clemson HGIC names April, just as summer growth begins, as the best time, recommends a container only slightly larger than the old one, and advises waiting several days after repotting before watering. Leather gloves or a band of folded newspaper keep the spines out of your hands.

Lay down newspaper, have the new pot and fresh commercial potting mix ready, and work through the steps below in one go so the roots do not dry out. Clemson HGIC recommends commercially prepared mix rather than garden soil, which carries pests and, its soil mix factsheet notes, too many bacteria for containers.
list: Turn the pot upside down with one hand spread over the soil, the stem between your index and middle fingers, and knock the rim against a solid edge until the root ball slides out.
Look at the roots. White, firm roots are healthy; dark, soft ones mean root rot, and white cottony fluff on the outside of the root ball can be root mealybugs.
Loosen the root ball so the roots are not locked in a tight mass. Unwind or cut circling roots, and if they are too tight to tease apart, score the sides of the root ball with a knife.
Scrape off the top inch of old mix if it carries a crusty white salt deposit, as the Illinois Extension advises.
Cover the drainage hole with a single piece of broken clay pot so mix does not wash out. Do not add a layer of gravel or shards: Clemson HGIC says it slows water movement through the pot.
Add enough dry mix to the bottom that the top of the root ball sits within 1 inch of the rim, at the same depth it grew before, with no mix piled on top of the original soil line.
Fill around the root ball and press the mix gently with your fingers. Do not pack it down, and never pack wet mix.
Water right away until water runs out of the drainage hole, repeating several times if the mix is peat-based, then empty the saucer.

paras: Clemson HGIC's rule is a pot 1 or 2 inches larger in diameter than the current one, and the calculator above applies it with a few refinements: 1 to 2 inches for pots up to about 10 inches, a 2 inch step for larger ones, and only 1 inch for plants that like a snug fit, such as succulents, epiphytes like the Christmas cactus, and anything whose guide says it prefers being crowded, like the peace lily. When the roots are not crowded at all, it recommends the same pot with fresh mix, which UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions also describes.

The reason for small steps is geometry. Soil volume grows with the cube of the diameter, so a modest increase in width means a large increase in wet mix around the roots. The table shows the calculator's figures for a standard tapered pot.

paras: A good mix lets water and air pass through quickly yet still holds enough moisture, which is how Clemson HGIC defines it. Most bagged mixes are soilless, built on peat moss or coconut coir with perlite or vermiculite, and arrive sterile and light; Clemson adds that coir should be rinsed thoroughly before use to avoid salinity problems. For foliage plants, its soil mix factsheet gives a home version of a commercial recipe: 2 parts pine bark, 1 part peat and 1 part sand. Succulents and cacti want something grittier, and Clemson suggests equal volumes of peat-based potting soil and very coarse sand or grit for cacti.

sections.h2: Drainage holes, cachepots and pot material
paras: Use a pot with a drainage hole. If the decorative container you love has none, Clemson HGIC recommends double-potting: keep the plant in a plain pot that drains and set it inside the decorative one on a layer of gravel, which holds the runoff below the inner pot. That gravel belongs in the outer container only, never in the pot holding the roots.

Material changes your watering. Clay is porous, so air moves through the walls and the mix dries faster, and Clemson notes that plants in nonporous plastic or glazed pots need water less often. A plant moving from plastic to terracotta will want checking sooner than before, and the reverse is true too.

sections.h2: Aftercare and plants too big to move
paras: Some leaf drop after repotting is normal: the Illinois Extension lists transplant shock among the causes of general leaf loss. Resist the urge to keep watering a plant that droops in the first days. Clemson HGIC explains that any injury to the roots reduces their ability to take up water, so a wilting, freshly repotted plant in moist mix needs time, not more water. Wait until the mix dries to the plant's usual depth, which the watering calculator in our watering guide estimates.

For a floor plant in a container you cannot realistically lift or tip, Clemson HGIC recommends topdressing instead: remove the top 2 or 3 inches of mix and replace it with fresh mix every other year or so. And sometimes the Illinois Extension's advice is the most sensible one: when an old plant has outgrown its space, propagate a new one from it or replace it.

faq.q: Should I water a plant before or after repotting?
faq.a: After. The Illinois Extension says to press the mix around the roots and water immediately, and Clemson HGIC recommends watering until the excess drains out, several times for peat-based mixes, which are hard to wet. Clemson also says to fill the pot with dry mix and never pack wet media. Cacti are the exception: Clemson advises waiting several days before the first watering.

faq.q: Can I repot a houseplant in winter?
faq.a: It is better to wait. Clemson HGIC advises repotting only during spring and summer while the plant is actively growing and specifically warns against repotting dormant plants. In winter, most houseplants are resting, so damaged roots recover slowly and fresh, wet mix stays wet longer. The exception is root rot, where waiting does more harm than repotting out of season.

faq.q: Is it a good idea to put rocks in the bottom of a pot?
faq.a: Not in a pot with a drainage hole. Clemson HGIC says a layer of clay pieces or rocks actually slows water movement through the pot; a single shard over the hole is enough to keep mix in. Gravel only makes sense in a decorative container without a hole, under an inner pot that drains, where it keeps the runoff away from the roots.

faq.q: Can I reuse old potting soil when repotting?
faq.a: Use fresh mix. The Illinois Extension says to replant into the new container with fresh potting mix, and UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions recommends swapping out old media even when a plant goes back into the same pot. Old mix can hold built-up salts, which UF/IFAS says fresh mix clears, and it may harbor pests. Never reuse mix from a plant that had root rot or a root pest.

faq.q: Why is my plant drooping after I repotted it?
faq.a: Roots are always disturbed in repotting, and Clemson HGIC notes that any root injury reduces how much water the plant can take up, so it wilts even in moist mix. The Illinois Extension calls this transplant shock and lists it among the causes of leaf drop. Keep it out of hot sun, do not add more water while the mix is still damp, and give the roots time to recover.

faq.q: How do I refresh a plant that is too big to repot?
faq.a: Topdress it. Clemson HGIC recommends removing the top 2 or 3 inches of potting mix from a large container and replacing it with fresh mix every other year or so. If a white salt crust has formed on the surface, the Illinois Extension advises scraping away the top inch. Topdressing renews the upper layer of mix without the risk of moving a heavy plant.
